h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: The L2 term is divided by batch size, so with tiny batches the effective penalty relative to the data gradient is much stronger and extra alpha tips the net into underfitting.
At slow learning rates wider nets make more function-space progress per step, partially compensating for undertraining within 243 epochs.
At low learning rates weights move little and shrinkage never reaches equilibrium within the budget, so raising alpha costs less accuracy.
Tiny batches give many noisy updates per epoch, and the noise compounds through extra layers to destabilize deeper stacks.
Stacking narrow ReLU layers creates bottlenecks and dead-unit collapse, so added depth helps less when layers are narrow.
Larger batches reduce gradient variance and the number of risky steps, softening the instability of high learning rates where the accuracy floor also compresses losses.
Large batches give few steps per epoch, so lowering the learning rate there leaves the net clearly undertrained.
Deeper ReLU stacks have sharper loss curvature and reach the edge of stability at smaller learning rates.
Narrow nets are already capacity-bound, so additional shrinkage pushes them into underfitting faster than redundant wide nets.
Shrinkage applied to every layer compounds multiplicatively through a three-layer stack, collapsing the signal more than in a single-layer net.
